subject: Anatomy
summary: The testis produces sperm and testosterone, housed in the scrotum to keep temperature optimal. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose torsion, cryptorchidism, and tumors, which are common emergencies and malignancies worldwide.

sections.p: The testis is a paired, oval organ that synthesises sperm and testosterone. It is external to the abdomen to maintain a temperature 2‑3 °C below core body temperature.
b: Key for male fertility and endocrine function
Protected by the scrotal wall and tunica vaginalis

sections.p: Each testis lies within the scrotal sac, suspended by the spermatic cord. The organ is covered by tunica albuginea, then tunica vaginalis (parietal and visceral layers). Inside, seminiferous tubules produce sperm, while interstitial Leydig cells secrete testosterone.
b: Tunica vaginalis: serous sac allowing movement

sections.p: Anteriorly the testis contacts the epididymis; posteriorly the pampiniform plexus drains venous blood. The spermatic cord contains vas deferens, vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
b: Spermatic cord: passes through inguinal canal

sections.p: Arterial blood arrives via the testicular artery (branch of the abdominal aorta) and the cremasteric and deferential arteries. Venous drainage is through the pampiniform plexus into the testicular vein (right drains to IVC, left to renal vein).
b: Venous drainage: pampiniform plexus → testicular vein

sections.p: Sensory innervation is via the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the ilioinguinal nerve. Autonomic fibers (sympathetic) travel with the testicular artery.
b: Genital branch of genitofemoral: cremasteric reflex

sections.p: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules under Sertoli cell support and hormonal regulation (FSH, LH, testosterone). Leydig cells produce testosterone, essential for secondary sexual characteristics and libido.

Common problems include cryptorchidism, torsion, infection, and germ‑cell tumours. Recognising anatomy guides rapid assessment and management, especially in low‑resource settings where imaging may be limited.
b: Cryptorchidism: ↑ cancer risk, orchiopexy before 2 y
Epididymitis: often infectious, treat before surgery

sections.p: Physical exam focuses on size, consistency, tenderness, and the cremasteric reflex. Absence of the reflex suggests torsion; a firm, non‑tender mass raises suspicion for tumour.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging, painless testicular mass (possible tumour)

faq.q: Why is the testis located outside the abdomen?
faq.a: External placement keeps temperature low enough for normal sperm production.

faq.q: What is the cremasteric reflex and its clinical use?
faq.a: Stroking the inner thigh causes the testis to rise; absent reflex suggests torsion.

faq.q: How does cryptorchidism increase cancer risk?
faq.a: Undescended testes are exposed to higher temperatures, leading to germ‑cell dysplasia and higher malignancy rates.

exam: Explain the blood supply of the testis and why left‑sided varicocele is more common.
Describe the steps in evaluating acute scrotal pain and the urgency of torsion.
Differentiate seminoma from non‑seminomatous germ‑cell tumours in terms of spread and markers.
